requirement: Yield checks and quantity reconciliations are to be performed as needed to show there are no discrepancies beyond acceptable limits; any significant departure from the expected yield must be recorded and investigated.
system_implications: REQUIRED by the text: the master defines yield/reconciliation checkpoints wherever the process needs them (5.8 says 'as necessary'), each with a theoretical basis, formula and acceptable limits; the system calculates the result from captured quantities (inputs, outputs, samples, rejects, waste, residues) and records it; a result outside the limit (i.e. a significant yield deviation) is recorded and investigated through a linked deviation. DESIGN CHOICES (not mandated by 5.8/5.44): separate alert and action limits; a hard block on moving to the next step until the deviation is opened/approved; holding batch disposition until the investigation closes (the release hold reflects Annex 16 certification expectations, not Ch.5). Examples - tablets: granule yield after drying/milling, tablet count vs theoretical, coating weight gain; injectables: compounded volume vs theoretical, filled units, lyophilised vials, visual-inspection rejects.
note: Clause numbers and paraphrase are correct. Implications re-labelled: Ch.5 only requires checks where necessary, a record, and investigation of significant yield deviations; blocking progression and holding disposition are design choices (the release hold is Annex 16-derived).

requirement: Before a processing operation starts, it must be confirmed that the area and equipment are clean and hold no materials, products, residues or paperwork unrelated to the operation about to begin.
system_implications: REQUIRED by the text: a clearance step before each processing operation starts; the system verifies electronically what it can (previous batch closed out in the room/equipment log, equipment status 'clean', no materials of other orders allocated to the room) and captures signed confirmation of the physical checks (no foreign materials, products, residues or documents). DESIGN CHOICES beyond 5.40: a formal checklist for processing clearance (Ch.5 mandates a checklist only for packaging line clearance, 5.50); an independent second-person verifier signature; repeating clearance after interruptions; clean-hold-time expiry checks (clean hold times come from cleaning validation under Annex 15, not from 5.40).
note: Clause and paraphrase correct. The original implication/test implied a checklist and two signatures; 5.40 requires neither, so both are marked as design choices, as is the clean-hold-time check (Annex 15).

requirement: Different products may only be handled in the same room at the same time, or back-to-back, if this has been shown to create no risk of mix-up or cross-contamination.
system_implications: Room/area occupancy control: the system tracks which batch/product occupies each room and refuses to start a second product in an occupied room unless the room is configured as segregated for concurrent work with a documented risk-assessment reference (the basis for 'no risk' should come from the 5.20 QRM). Consecutive use by a different product requires completed cleaning and clearance before the room returns to 'available'. DESIGN CHOICE: requiring QA approval of the concurrent-use configuration.
note: Clause and paraphrase correct ('shown' is an interpretive but reasonable reading: absence of risk needs a documented basis). Implications are within scope; only the QA-approval step is flagged as a design choice.

requirement: During processing, every material, bulk container, major equipment item and, where appropriate, room must carry a label or other identification showing the product or material, strength where relevant, batch number and, where applicable, the production stage. Labels must be unambiguous, easy to read and follow the company's standard layout; colours signalling status (such as quarantine, approved, rejected or cleaned) are an optional extra aid.
system_implications: REQUIRED minimum (5.12): product/material, strength where applicable, batch number, stage where applicable; identification may be a physical label OR another means such as an electronic status display, because 5.12 allows items to be 'otherwise identified'. 5.13: label templates are the company's agreed format (keep them under change control), clear and unambiguous; colour coding of status is optional ('often helpful'). DESIGN CHOICES: system-generated labels from batch data with a barcode/2D code; extra fields (container n of N, gross/tare/net, status, date/time, user); room/equipment status displays ('In use - product/batch/stage', 'Cleaned', 'To be cleaned'); scan-based identity checks at each step; forced relabel/reprint on status change with audit trail.
note: Minor correction. Clause numbers correct (5.13 verified as the label-format/colour clause). Wording changed from 'recommended' to 'optional': the text only says colour coding is often helpful. Implications re-labelled: barcodes, scanning and extra label fields are design choices, and non-label identification is permitted by 5.12.

requirement: Deviating from instructions or procedures is to be kept to a minimum; when a deviation does happen, a competent person must give written approval, with Quality Control involved when relevant.
system_implications: REQUIRED by the text: recipe enforcement keeps departures to a minimum (sequence, limits, material identity); any departure (parameter outside range, skipped step, alternative equipment) is possible only through an in-line deviation record (description, impact) approved by the e-signature of a person designated as competent for that deviation class - an Annex 11/Ch.4-compliant e-signature satisfies 'approved in writing'; QC involvement is routed for deviation classes configured as quality-relevant. The deviation ID is linked to the step and appears in the batch record. DESIGN CHOICES beyond 5.15: routing to QA (the text names QC); forbidding operator self-approval (segregation of duties); blocking batch release while linked deviations are open (that hold follows Annex 16 certification prerequisites, not 5.15).
note: Clause and paraphrase correct. Implications re-labelled: 5.15 only requires written approval by a competent person with QC involvement when appropriate; no-self-approval and the release block are design choices / Annex 16-derived.

requirement: Dispensing of starting materials is restricted to designated staff working to a written procedure, so that the right material in the right quantity ends up in clean, correctly labelled containers. An independent second check of each dispensed item and its quantity is required and must be documented. Everything dispensed for one batch is kept as a group and visibly labelled as belonging to that batch.
system_implications: Dispensing module: only users designated as dispensers (designation evidenced e.g. by role plus current training - the training interlock is a design choice) can dispense, following the procedure embedded in the step; material lot scanned and checked against the BOM, released status and retest/expiry (these status checks implement 5.34); weight/volume captured from a balance/meter with tolerance check against target (balance calibration/checks come from Ch.3, not Ch.5); container label printed automatically. The independent check (5.38) is recorded either as a second-person e-signature by a different user or as a validated automated check (barcode + balance interface) - 5.38 requires independence and a record but does not specify a second person. Dispensed items grouped into a batch kit with a conspicuous kit label and a completeness check before issue. Product-specific: WFI, pH adjusters and filter/stopper components (injectables); potency-adjusted API with compensating excipient (tablets).
note: Clauses and paraphrase correct. Implications re-labelled: training interlock, daily balance checks and potency adjustment are design/other-source items; a validated system check is a defensible alternative to a second person because the text does not mandate one.

requirement: Contamination of a starting material or product by another material or product must be prevented. The risk of accidental cross-contamination (airborne release such as dust or vapour, biological material, residues left on equipment, operators' clothing) must be assessed, bearing in mind that injectables and long-term therapies are the most sensitive although all products are at risk. Control relies on premises/equipment design (Ch.3) supported by process design and technical/organisational measures, including effective and reproducible cleaning. A QRM process that includes a potency and toxicological evaluation of the products (and considers facility/equipment design, personnel and material flows, microbiological controls, API properties, process, cleaning and analytical capability) decides whether and how far premises, equipment or product-contact parts must be dedicated, or whether a segregated self-contained area is justified, and how extensive the technical and organisational measures must be; Ch.5 gives these measures as examples, not a mandatory set. The measures and their effectiveness must be reviewed periodically under set procedures. Making non-medicinal products in medicinal areas/equipment should normally be avoided and is only acceptable where justified and controlled; technical poisons such as pesticides and herbicides must not be made or stored in medicinal manufacturing/storage areas (unless used to make medicines).
system_implications: Product master carries the QRM outputs: HBEL/PDE-based cleaning limits (the HBEL approach is the EMA guideline tied to this chapter's implementation dates), dedication flags for facility/area/equipment and for specific product-contact parts (e.g. tablet punches/dies, filters, filling needles, hoses, maintenance tools), allowed rooms/equipment, campaign rules, required cleaning procedure and whether cleaning verification is required. Execution enforces them: only permitted rooms/equipment/parts selectable; a changeover matrix sets the cleaning level; single-use assemblies (injectables) cannot be reused; where the QRM requires post-campaign cleaning verification, the result must be recorded before the equipment is released to another product. Any non-medicinal product is flagged so it cannot be scheduled on medicinal equipment without a recorded justification. A periodic review report (cleaning failures, changeovers, spills/events, EM excursions) supports the 5.22 review. CORRECTIONS vs original: cleaning verification is NOT required at every changeover by Ch.5 - 5.21 presents it as a detectability measure to consider for higher-risk products after a campaign; campaign-length limits are a design choice.
note: Clause range right but paraphrase understated: it omitted the potency part of the evaluation, the 5.18 risk-assessment content (sources; injectables/long-term products most sensitive), that the 5.21 measures are QRM-selected examples, the 'set procedures' for periodic review, the 'where justified' allowance for non-medicinal products and the absolute ban on technical poisons. The implication overstated cleaning verification as universal.

requirement: Packaging programmes must be planned to minimise risks of cross-contamination, mix-up or substitution; different products are not packaged close to each other unless physically segregated. The product name and batch number being packed must be displayed at every packaging station or line.
system_implications: REQUIRED by the text: line/room model with segregation attributes so that the scheduler/execution refuses to run a different product on an adjacent line that is not physically segregated; each packaging station or line (every station where a line has several, e.g. blister machine, cartoner, labeller, case packer) shows at least the product name and batch number of the active order. DESIGN CHOICES: using an electronic HMI/screen rather than a physical line board (either satisfies 5.51); adding strength, pack and status; clearing the display only after order close and line clearance.
note: Both clause numbers verified as correct (they had been flagged uncertain). Implication adjusted: the text requires only name and batch number at each station or line; an electronic display and the extra fields are design choices.

requirement: Before packaging starts, the work area, packaging lines, printers and other equipment must be verified clean and free of any product, material or document from earlier work that is not needed now; this line clearance follows an appropriate checklist.
system_implications: REQUIRED by the text: packaging order has a mandatory first step 'line clearance' performed against a master-defined, line-specific checklist (e.g. feeder hoppers, reject bins, printer ribbons/plates, vision-system recipe, floor/under-machine areas, documents removed). DESIGN CHOICES (not mandated by 5.50, though a common inspector expectation for mix-up risk): each item individually confirmed; performer plus independent verifier signatures by two different users; an electronic check that the previous order on the line is closed and reconciled and that no components of another order remain allocated to the line; blocking any packaging step, printer job or line start until clearance is signed.
note: Clause and paraphrase correct. The original implication already marked the dual signature as a design choice; the previous-order/reconciliation interlock is now also marked as a design choice.

requirement: On arrival at the packaging area, every product and packaging component must be checked to confirm the right quantity, the right identity and agreement with the packaging instructions.
system_implications: REQUIRED by the text: receipt-at-line step in which each bulk container and packaging-component lot is checked for quantity, identity (item code, artwork/version) and conformity with the packaging instructions/BOM, with the result recorded; received quantities posted to the order's reconciliation ledger. The released-status and expiry check supports 5.5 (quarantine until released for use) rather than 5.52. DESIGN CHOICES: scan-based checking and a hard block of the step on any mismatch.
note: Clause and paraphrase correct. Implication kept; the status check is attributed to 5.5 and blocking is marked as a design choice.

requirement: Containers must be clean when they are filled - the text sets the condition, not an in-house washing step, so supplier-cleaned ready-to-use containers can qualify - and care must be taken to avoid and remove foreign matter such as glass or metal particles. Filling and sealing should normally be followed by labelling as soon as possible; where that is not the case, procedures must prevent mix-ups and wrong labels.
system_implications: REQUIRED by the text: the cleanliness basis of each container/component lot is established before filling, and foreign-matter controls are applied (recorded where the master defines them as checks). Unlabelled filled units (e.g. vials held for inspection before labelling) are managed under a procedure that prevents mix-ups: tracked as 'bright stock' with unique tray/container IDs, location, count and hold start; a labelling order can only consume bright stock of the matching batch, verified by scan. SOURCED ELSEWHERE: for injectables, washing/depyrogenation/sterilisation records and their hold-time limits (and blocking filling when they expire) implement Annex 1, not Ch.5. NOT MANDATED: a container-washing step for tablet bottles - supplier-clean bottles with any air-rinse/inversion step defined by the master are acceptable. DESIGN CHOICE: configurable maximum filling-to-labelling interval with an alert (the text only says 'as quickly as possible' normally).
note: Clauses correct. Wording corrected from 'must be cleaned before filling' to 'must be clean' - the text states a condition, which matters for RTU vials and supplier-clean bottles. Depyrogenation/sterile hold-time controls re-attributed to Annex 1; the filling-to-labelling time limit is a design choice.

requirement: Printed packaging materials need particular care: they are stored securely so that unauthorised people cannot get to them, and cut labels and other loose printed items are kept and moved in separate closed containers to avoid mix-ups. Issue of packaging materials of any kind (not only printed ones) is limited to authorised staff working to an approved, documented procedure. Each incoming lot or delivery of primary or printed packaging is given its own reference number or identifying mark. Outdated or obsolete primary or printed packaging material must be destroyed and the disposal recorded.
system_implications: REQUIRED by the text: access-controlled storage locations for printed materials; the packaging-material issue transaction (all packaging materials) restricted to an authorised role and executed per the approved procedure; each delivery/batch of printed or primary material carries its own internal reference, and each issued unit (reel, carton bundle, sealed box of cut labels) is scanned by that reference and linked to the order, with the closed-container ID recorded for cut labels; outdated or obsolete stock is destroyed with a record (quantity, method, date, performer). The obsolescence logic must cover BOTH superseded artwork versions AND outdated primary/printed material past its expiry or retest date (e.g. stoppers, vials, blister foil, labels) - the original covered only artwork changes. DESIGN CHOICES: automatic blocking/routing of such stock to a destruction task, and a witness signature (5.48 requires only destruction plus a record).
note: Clauses correct. Scope corrected: the issue-control sentence of 5.46 applies to all packaging materials, not only printed ones; 5.48 covers outdated (expired) primary packaging as well as obsolete artwork. Witnessed destruction re-labelled as a design choice.

requirement: Correct execution of every printing operation (e.g. batch code, expiry date), whether done separately or during packaging, must be checked and recorded, and any hand printing re-checked at regular intervals. Extra care is required with cut labels and with off-line overprinting; roll-fed labels are normally preferred over cut labels to help avoid mix-ups.
system_implications: REQUIRED by the text: every printing/coding operation (in-line or off-line) is checked and the check recorded; hand printing has a recurring re-check at a configured interval with overdue alerting; cut-label use and off-line overprinting are flagged in the master as operations needing additional controls. DESIGN CHOICES: variable print data sent electronically from the batch record to printers/coders (no manual keying); expiry calculated from a master shelf-life rule; start-of-run and periodic verification with specimen images; 100% vision or dual verification as the extra control for cut labels/off-line overprint; invalidating a print job when batch data change after set-up; blocking production mode until the start-up print check is recorded.
note: Clauses and paraphrase correct (the roll-feed preference in 5.56 is advisory). Implications re-labelled: most mechanisms are design choices supporting the required check-and-record.

requirement: The correct operation of electronic code readers, label counters and comparable devices must be checked. Printed or embossed information on packs must be clear and must not easily fade or rub off.
system_implications: REQUIRED by the text: documented checks that code readers, label counters and similar devices work correctly; printed/embossed information on packaging materials is distinct and resistant to fading or erasure - a property controlled through the packaging-material specification and print-quality checks. DESIGN CHOICES: challenge tests with deliberate wrong-code/missing-label/unreadable-code/missing-leaflet pieces at start-up, after interventions/stoppages and at end of run; blocking production mode on a missing or failed challenge; counting challenge pieces out and back in; 2D-code grading and rub-resistance tests recorded as IPCs.
note: Clauses and paraphrase correct. Ch.5 sets no challenge frequency and no blocking rule; these are re-labelled as design choices.

requirement: During packaging, on-line checks must at least confirm that finished packs look right and are complete, that the correct product and components are being used and any overprint is right, and that line monitoring devices are working. Units taken off the line as samples must never be put back.
system_implications: REQUIRED by the text: the packaging master's IPC plan contains, as a minimum, the 5.59 check categories (pack appearance, completeness, correct product/materials, correct overprint, line-monitor function) at a defined frequency with pass/fail and sample counts; samples withdrawn are recorded by quantity and purpose and deducted in reconciliation, and the system offers no transaction to return sampled units to the line. DESIGN CHOICES: alerts for missed IPCs. BEYOND the 5.59 minimum (product-specific or Annex 1): container-closure checks such as crimp/seal and vial label placement (injectables); blister seal integrity/leak tests and count per bottle (tablets).
note: Clause and paraphrase correct. Product-specific checks are kept but flagged as going beyond the 5.59 minimum.

requirement: If product is caught up in an unusual event (e.g. jam, spill, dropped units, suspected mix-up), it may re-enter the process only after it has been specially inspected, the event investigated, and authorised staff have approved; this must be documented in detail.
system_implications: REQUIRED by the text: a 'set-aside/unusual event' transaction in which affected units are counted and held in a set-aside bucket linked to an event record (what happened, time, quantity, location); reintroduction requires an inspection result, an investigation reference and approval by an authorised role, all recorded in detail; quantities flow into reconciliation. DESIGN CHOICES: forbidding the operator who raised the event from approving it; defaulting non-reintroduced units to reject.
note: Clause and paraphrase correct. Only the segregation-of-duties rule and the default-to-reject route are re-labelled as design choices.

requirement: Any significant or unusual discrepancy found when reconciling bulk quantity and printed packaging materials against units produced must be investigated and satisfactorily explained before the batch is released.
system_implications: REQUIRED by the text: end-of-order reconciliation of bulk product and printed packaging materials against units produced (issued = used + destroyed + returned + samples + rejects + set-aside), with master-defined limits that define a 'significant' discrepancy; an out-of-limit result requires a linked investigation, and release/certification is blocked until it is satisfactorily accounted for. DESIGN CHOICES: zero tolerance for batch-coded printed items; blocking order close as well as release; requiring QA as the approver of the investigation. Examples - tablets: bulk tablets by weight/count vs packs; injectables: filled/inspected units vs labelled units vs cartons.
note: Clause and paraphrase correct; the release block is required by the text, the order-close block and QA approver are design choices.

requirement: When packaging is finished, any unused packaging material already coded with the batch must be destroyed and the destruction recorded; returning uncoded printed materials to stock must follow a documented procedure.
system_implications: REQUIRED by the text: order close-out distinguishes batch-coded from uncoded leftovers (based on whether in-line/off-line coding occurred); coded leftovers go to a destruction record (quantity, method, date, performer) and can never be returned to stock; uncoded printed leftovers can be returned only through a return-to-stock transaction that embodies the documented procedure (count, container relabelling, update of the component lot quantity). DESIGN CHOICES: a witness signature on destruction; QA/stores acceptance and a count-verification signature on returns.
note: Clause and paraphrase correct; witness and acceptance signatures re-labelled as design choices.

requirement: Necessary in-process and environmental controls must be performed and recorded, and intermediate and bulk products must be held under appropriate conditions.
system_implications: REQUIRED by the text: IPCs and environmental controls defined as necessary in the master (frequency, sample size, limits) are performed and recorded (automatic capture from balances, hardness/thickness testers, checkweighers, fill-weight systems, pH/conductivity meters where possible); intermediate/bulk holds record container, location and storage condition. DESIGN CHOICES: alerts for missed IPCs; linking room environmental data (temperature/RH, particle counts, pressures) by time window; pulling excursions into the exception report and blocking QA review completion until assessed. SOURCED ELSEWHERE: maximum hold times for intermediates/bulk come from process validation/hold-time studies and the MA dossier, grade A/B viable and non-viable monitoring and pre-filtration bioburden limits come from Annex 1 - Ch.5 only requires 'appropriate conditions' and that necessary controls are done and recorded.
note: Clauses and paraphrase correct. Implications re-attributed: hold-time limits come from validation studies/the MA and aseptic EM requirements from Annex 1, and the review block is a design choice.

requirement: Rejected materials and products must be clearly marked as rejected and segregated in restricted-access storage. Their fate (return to supplier, reprocessing where appropriate, or destruction) must be approved and documented by authorised people.
system_implications: REQUIRED by the text: 'Rejected' is a hard system status that blocks every consumption, issue, packaging and shipping transaction and is shown on the label; rejected stock must be physically moved to a restricted, separate location (unlike quarantine under 5.5, Ch.5 offers no purely administrative alternative for rejected goods, so the electronic status complements but does not replace physical segregation); the disposition (return to supplier / reprocess / destroy) is approved by an authorised role and the executed action and quantities are recorded. In-process rejects (e.g. checkweigher rejects, vials rejected at visual inspection) are counted into identified reject containers and follow the same path.
note: Clause and paraphrase correct. Implication clarified that physical segregation in a restricted area is required and cannot be satisfied by system status alone.

requirement: Reprocessing of rejected product is to be exceptional: allowed only when final quality is unaffected, specifications are met, and it follows a defined, authorised procedure after risk evaluation; a record of the reprocessing must be kept.
system_implications: REQUIRED by the text: reprocessing can only be executed from a pre-approved reprocessing procedure/master linked to the product (never ad hoc), launched after a documented risk evaluation; the reprocessing record is linked to the original batch genealogy and flagged for release review; conformity with specifications is confirmed before release. Also capture the QC decision on additional testing required by 5.69 for reprocessed batches (see EU5-22). SOURCED ELSEWHERE: restrictions on reprocessing sterile products (e.g. re-filtration only if validated and registered) come from the marketing authorisation and Annex 1, not Ch.5 - the per-product ability to disable reprocessing masters is a design choice. DESIGN CHOICE: launching reprocessing from an approved deviation/change record.
note: Clause and paraphrase correct. Sterile-product reprocessing limits re-attributed to MA/Annex 1; the 5.69 QC testing decision is added for reprocessed batches, which the original implications only covered for recovered material.

requirement: Adding all or part of earlier batches that meet quality requirements into a later batch of that same product, at a predefined manufacturing stage, needs prior authorisation, must follow a defined procedure after assessing risks (including any effect on shelf life), and must be recorded. QC must decide whether reprocessed product, or product containing recovered material, needs extra testing.
system_implications: REQUIRED by the text: recovered-material addition is a specific step type available only where the master defines it (defined stage); the source batch must be the same product and of conforming quality; authorisation is recorded before the addition; the procedure's risk evaluation (including shelf-life effect) is referenced; genealogy records source batch IDs and quantities; a QC decision on additional testing is a mandatory field before release for BOTH recovered-material batches and reprocessed batches (5.69 covers both). DESIGN CHOICES: a maximum proportion and batch-age limits in the master; calculating the receiving batch expiry from the oldest contributing batch (one way of implementing the shelf-life evaluation).
note: Clauses and paraphrase correct. Implication extended so the 5.69 QC decision also applies to reprocessed batches; age/proportion limits and the expiry rule re-labelled as design choices.

requirement: Market returns that have been outside the manufacturer's control default to destruction unless their quality is not in doubt. Resale, relabelling or use in a later batch is allowed only after QC has critically assessed them under a written procedure, considering the product type, any special storage needs, its condition and history, and how long it has been out. If quality is doubtful the goods must not be reissued or reused (though basic chemical recovery of the active substance may be possible). All actions must be recorded.
system_implications: Returned-goods receipt creates a quarantined 'returned' lot linked to the original batch; disposition requires a QC assessment record (nature of product, storage requirements and history - e.g. cold chain for injectables - condition, time since issue) and QC e-signature; default disposition is destroy. Returned units cannot be relabelled, resold or used as recovered material unless the assessment permits it; if doubt is recorded only destruction (or a chemical-recovery route) is available. The resulting action is recorded against the original batch history.
note: Clause and paraphrase correct; implications are within scope and kept (lightly reworded).

requirement: Incoming materials and finished products must be quarantined, physically or administratively, as soon as they are received or produced, and stay so until released for use or distribution. Finished products remain in quarantine, under conditions set by the manufacturer, until final release; the evaluation of product and documentation needed before release is governed by Ch.6. After release they are held as usable stock, again under manufacturer-set storage conditions. (QP certification is required by Directive 2001/83/EC Art. 51 and Annex 16, not by Ch.5.)
system_implications: Every produced lot is created in 'Quarantine' at the moment its output is posted (5.5 'immediately'); the change to 'Released' is only possible through the release transaction after record review is complete (steps signed, deviations closed, reconciliation passed, lab results approved) - these prerequisites come from Ch.6 and Annex 16, and the QP-certification step is an Annex 16 requirement. Interfaces to ERP/WMS must respect status (no allocation or shipment of quarantined stock). Administrative (electronic) quarantine is acceptable under 5.5 provided the system enforces it. Storage-condition attributes of the finished product apply both before and after release.
note: Clauses correct. Paraphrase corrected: QP certification had been attributed to Ch.5 but comes from Art. 51 of Directive 2001/83/EC and Annex 16; added the 'immediately after receipt or processing' timing of 5.5 and the post-release storage-condition requirement of 5.65.

requirement: Throughout every processing stage, products and materials must be protected against microbial and other contamination. When dry materials and products are handled, special precautions must stop dust from being generated and spreading, above all for highly active (potent) or sensitising materials.
system_implications: Ch.5 states the protection objective only; the mechanisms are design choices or come from other texts. Tablets (design choices consistent with 5.11/5.21): the master can require dust-control prerequisites before open-handling steps (local extraction/containment on, pressure cascade OK, contained transfer connected) as signed checks or interface signals; potent-API weighing only in designated booths. Injectables (SOURCED FROM Annex 1, not Ch.5): aseptic prerequisites before exposure steps (grade A airflow/particle status, sterile equipment within hold time, gowning qualification valid, interventions logged) and bioburden/time limits for non-sterile bulk solution before sterile filtration - keep them but trace them to Annex 1.
note: Clauses correct. Wording corrected: the text refers to 'highly active' (i.e. potent) materials, not 'highly hazardous' ones. Injectable aseptic controls in the implication re-attributed to Annex 1.

requirement: Checks must confirm that pipelines and other equipment that transfer product from one area to another are correctly connected.
system_implications: REQUIRED by the text: transfer steps (e.g. bulk solution from compounding vessel to filling line via transfer panel/hoses; vacuum/pneumatic powder transfer to a tablet press hopper) include a connection check before transfer, recorded in the batch record (recording follows from 5.2). DESIGN CHOICES: scanning source vessel, panel/hose/port and destination IDs, or reading panel proximity sensors, and comparing them with the master route; blocking the transfer on mismatch; a second-person verifier signature (5.14 requires a check, not two people).
note: Clause and paraphrase correct. The verifier signature and interlocks re-labelled as design choices.

requirement: Starting materials in the storage area must be suitably labelled with at least the designated material name (plus the internal code where applicable) and the batch number assigned at receipt, and, where relevant, the lot's QC status (for instance quarantine, under test, released or rejected) and its expiry or retest date; when a fully computerised storage system is used, this information need not all be legible on the label. Procedures or measures must make sure every container holds what it is supposed to hold, and bulk containers that have been sampled must be identified as such. Only starting materials released by QC and still within their retest period may be used.
system_implications: The eBMR relies on (or provides) a validated inventory status as the master for material status; at dispensing and at charging, each container scan checks identity (item code), released status, retest/expiry date and, where Annex 8 requires it, container-level identity-test status (5.35 requires at least identity testing of each batch per Annex 8). The sampling transaction sets a 'sampled' flag on the container, shown on its label/record and at dispensing (5.33, see Ch.6). If labels carry only a barcode, the system is the authoritative source for the omitted data and must be validated for that purpose (Annex 11).
note: Clauses correct. Paraphrase understated: it omitted the internal code reference, that status and expiry/retest are required only 'where appropriate', and the 5.33 requirement to identify sampled bulk containers; all added, with the matching sampled-container flag in the implications.

requirement: Production must be carried out and overseen by competent staff, and every handling activity for materials and products, from goods receipt through processing and packaging to distribution, must follow written procedures or instructions and be recorded where necessary.
system_implications: REQUIRED by the text: each master step is executed according to, and links to, the governing procedure/instruction version; handling activities that need a record are captured in the batch record; performer and supervisor/verifier roles are distinct permissions so that competent people perform and supervise. DESIGN CHOICE (one way to evidence competence; training requirements themselves sit in Ch.2): each step declares the required qualification per procedure version and the system checks the user's current training status (LMS interface or internal records) before allowing them to perform or verify the step.
note: Clauses and paraphrase correct. The training-status interlock is re-labelled as a design choice: 5.1 requires competent people but prescribes no mechanism.

requirement: Validation studies must be run according to defined procedures, with results and conclusions recorded. When a new formula or preparation method is introduced, it must be demonstrated fit for routine production: run as defined with the specified materials and equipment, the process must reliably deliver product of the required quality. Significant changes to the process (including equipment or material changes) that may affect product quality or reproducibility must be validated; critical processes must be validated (5.42); and processes and procedures must undergo periodic critical re-validation to confirm they still achieve the intended results.
system_implications: REQUIRED support: master recipes record the validation basis of the process; process-impacting master changes (CPP ranges, equipment class, materials/suppliers, batch size, sequence) cannot be approved without a linked change-control and validation reference. DESIGN CHOICES: classifying every master change as editorial vs process-impacting; a master comparison (diff) report. SOURCED ELSEWHERE: flagging batches made under a master still in validation (PPQ/concurrent batches) and conditioning their release on the validation outcome follows Annex 15, not Ch.5. Periodic re-validation is a QMS activity; the eBMR can support it with batch-data trend reports.
note: Clause set extended with 5.42 (critical processes validated), which no original line cited. Paraphrase corrected: the text requires periodic critical re-validation of processes and procedures (not merely 'reassessment'), recording of conclusions as well as results, and consistent quality using the specified materials and equipment. PPQ release control re-attributed to Annex 15.

requirement: The manufacturer must promptly tell the marketing authorisation holder about manufacturing constraints that could cause an abnormal restriction of supply, so the MAH can notify the competent authorities.
system_implications: Organisational duty; no eBMR function is mandated. Optional support (design choice): batch/campaign rejection, prolonged line holds or major deviations can carry a 'potential supply impact' attribute that creates a notification task to the supply/QA contact for the MAH, with timestamped acknowledgement.
note: Clause and paraphrase correct (5.71 is the 2015 addition on supply restrictions; the MAH's reporting duty stems from Directive 2001/83/EC, Articles 23a and 81). eBMR support is optional.

requirement: Manufacturing must be carried out to clearly defined procedures and in line with GMP so that products reach the required quality, and it must match what the site's manufacturing authorisation and the product's marketing authorisation (MA) allow.
system_implications: Master recipes and packaging instructions carry the MA reference (product, MA number, market) and the registered data they must respect (formula, batch size or range, registered process parameters and IPC limits, specifications, shelf life). Master approval includes a documented regulatory-conformity sign-off; a master cannot set limits wider than the registered values without a linked regulatory-variation reference; batches can only be created from an approved, effective master version valid for the target market. DESIGN CHOICES: the approval roles, the hard block on registered ranges, and sourcing MA data from a regulatory information system by interface.
verification_test: Try to approve a master revision whose CPP range is wider than the registered range with no variation reference -> blocked. Create a batch for a market not linked to the master's MA -> refused. The batch record shows the master version and MA reference used.

requirement: Every incoming consignment must be checked to confirm it matches the order, and containers are cleaned where needed and labelled with the prescribed information. For each delivery of starting material, every container is checked for package integrity (including any tamper-evident seal) and the delivery note, purchase order and supplier labels are checked against each other and against the manufacturer's own approved manufacturer/supplier records; these receiving checks are documented.
system_implications: If the MES/WMS performs goods receipt: a receipt transaction records the order match, a per-container integrity/seal check and any cleaning, compares the manufacturer and supplier shown on the delivery documents/labels with the approved-source master data (mismatch -> lot blocked and routed to QC; see EUB-NEW-09), prints receipt labels with the prescribed data, and signs off the documented checks. If receipt is done in ERP/WMS: the eBMR accepts for dispensing/issue only lots whose receipt checks are flagged complete through the interface. DESIGN CHOICES: the automatic comparison and the blocking.
verification_test: Receive a lot whose supplier label names a manufacturer not on the approved list -> lot blocked for QC. Try to dispense from a lot whose receipt checks are not recorded as complete -> refused. The receipt record shows each check with user and time.

requirement: Any damage to containers, or any other problem that could harm a material's quality, must be investigated, recorded and reported to the QC department.
system_implications: At receipt, storage, dispensing and charging, users can raise a 'material/container problem' record against the specific container (damaged or leaking container, broken seal, signs of contamination, abnormal appearance); QC is notified automatically and the investigation outcome is recorded against the lot. DESIGN CHOICE: automatic hold of the container (optionally the whole lot) until QC records a disposition.
verification_test: During dispensing, report a damaged drum -> record created, QC notified, container blocked; attempt to dispense from it before QC disposition -> refused; the QC disposition and investigation appear in the lot history.

requirement: Bought-in intermediates and bulk products are to be treated at receipt exactly like starting materials.
system_implications: Purchased intermediates/bulk (e.g. bought-in bulk tablets for packaging; a bought-in intermediate or bulk solution for filling) go through the starting-material flow: quarantine on receipt, receipt checks, sampling/identity testing, QC release, identity labelling and approved-source check before they can be issued to a processing or packaging order; the genealogy links the external lot and its manufacturer batch number to the finished batch.
verification_test: Issue a purchased bulk lot still in quarantine to a packaging order -> refused. After QC release it can be issued and appears in the genealogy with the supplier's batch number.

requirement: All materials and products must be kept under the storage conditions the manufacturer has defined, and stored in an orderly way that allows batches to be kept apart and stock to be rotated.
system_implications: The material/product master holds storage conditions; storage, staging and line-side locations managed by the MES carry condition attributes, and the system prevents placing a lot in a location with incompatible conditions (e.g. 2-8 C material in ambient staging). Lot/container-level location tracking keeps batches segregated. DESIGN CHOICES: FEFO/FIFO picking proposals with a recorded reason for any override; time-out-of-storage tracking for temperature-sensitive materials.
verification_test: Try to stage a 2-8 C material in an ambient location -> blocked. Picking proposes the earliest-expiry released lot; selecting another requires a recorded reason.

requirement: Only authorised staff may enter production areas.
system_implications: Primarily a facility/physical access-control measure; the eBMR supports rather than enforces it. Support: an area-authorisation list per room/area; a user can perform or sign steps executed in a restricted area only if authorised for that area (for aseptic areas also a valid gowning qualification, which is an Annex 1 requirement); optional interface to the access-control system to cross-check that the signer was badged into the room. DESIGN CHOICES: all of these enforcement mechanisms.
verification_test: A user not authorised for the filling suite attempts to sign a filling step -> refused. After an authorisation is withdrawn, the user can no longer sign steps in that area.

clause: Ch.5 5.19; 5.21 (organisational measures on campaign cleaning, cleaning verification, cleaning records and status labels; technical measure on validated clean-in-place); with Ch.4 4.31
requirement: Cleaning processes must be effective and reproducible (5.19). Among the cross-contamination measures chosen through QRM, 5.21 lists: detailed cleaning records designed to prove cleaning was completed per the approved procedure; status labels showing the cleaning state of rooms and equipment; campaign working ended by cleaning of validated effectiveness; post-campaign cleaning verification for higher-risk products; and automatic clean-in-place of validated effectiveness. Combined with Ch.4 4.31 (logbooks recording cleaning of production equipment and areas), electronic cleaning records and cleaning-status indication are a baseline eBMR/MES function rather than an option.
system_implications: Electronic equipment/room logbook: each cleaning (manual cleaning, CIP/SIP cycles on injectable compounding/filling equipment, parts washing in common wash areas) is recorded against the equipment/room with cleaning type, procedure version, start/end and performer, and for automated cycles the cycle data and pass/fail. Equipment/room status (in use, to be cleaned, cleaned, product last processed) is derived from these records and shown on the status label/display, so nothing can show 'clean' without a completed record. Campaign counters and end-of-campaign cleaning are enforced where the QRM defines campaigns; post-campaign verification results are recorded where the QRM requires them. DESIGN CHOICES: second-person check of cleaning; clean-hold-time expiry (Annex 15 cleaning validation).
verification_test: Try to set equipment status to 'clean' without a completed cleaning record for the current procedure version -> impossible. Equipment used for product A and not cleaned cannot be allocated to product B, and its display shows 'to be cleaned - product A, batch X'. A failed CIP cycle leaves the vessel in 'to be cleaned'.

clause: Ch.5 5.21 (organisational measure on recording spills, accidental events and procedural deviations); see also 5.15, 5.22
requirement: As one of the QRM-selected organisational controls against cross-contamination, spills, accidental events and departures from procedures are to be recorded.
system_implications: An event log available from every processing and packaging step (spill, container breakage, filter/bag rupture, powder release, containment breach, equipment failure with product exposure) captures location, materials/batches affected, quantity and immediate clean-up actions; it is linked to the batch record and to the room/equipment logbook, and the affected room/equipment is set to 'cleaning required'. Events that are departures from procedure feed the deviation process (5.15), and all events feed the periodic review of cross-contamination measures (5.22). DESIGN CHOICE: blocking further steps in the room until cleaning is recorded.
verification_test: Log a powder spill in the granulation suite -> event appears in the batch record and exception report, room status changes to 'cleaning required', and (if configured) the next step in that room is blocked until cleaning is recorded. The periodic review report lists the event.

requirement: Choosing, qualifying, approving and maintaining suppliers of starting materials, and of primary and printed packaging materials, must be documented within the PQS, with oversight proportionate to each material's risk and supporting evidence kept; where possible, starting materials are bought directly from their manufacturer. For active substances, supply-chain traceability back to the active-substance starting materials must be established, its risks formally assessed and periodically verified, and the traceability records held by the EEA manufacturer or importer; API manufacturers and distributors are audited for GMP/GDP compliance at risk-based intervals. Excipients and their suppliers are controlled on the basis of a formalised risk assessment.
system_implications: Largely QMS/ERP: audits, quality agreements (5.28) and excipient risk assessments need no eBMR function. eBMR/MES support: the material master holds approved manufacturer/supplier combinations for starting and primary/printed packaging materials with their approval status, and lots from unapproved or suspended sources are blocked at receipt and at dispensing/issue (interface check); batch genealogy records for every API lot its manufacturer, supplier/distributor and manufacturer batch number, so traceability from a finished batch back to the API source can be produced on demand. DESIGN CHOICE: repeating the source check at dispensing as well as at receipt.
verification_test: Suspend an API manufacturer in the approved-source list -> its lots can no longer be received or dispensed. The genealogy report for a finished batch lists each API lot with manufacturer, supplier and manufacturer batch number.

requirement: When a single delivery of a material contains several batches, each batch is to be handled on its own for sampling, testing and release.
system_implications: Receipt creates a separate internal lot for each supplier batch in the delivery; sampling plans, test results and QC status are held per lot; dispensing and genealogy reference the internal lot mapped to its supplier batch; the system does not allow one internal lot to span two supplier batches, nor a whole delivery to be released in a single action.
verification_test: Receive one delivery containing three supplier batches -> three internal lots created; releasing one leaves the other two in quarantine; an attempt to book two supplier batches into one internal lot -> refused.
